features.name: Buffalo Zoo
features.description: Buffalo Zoo is a mapped museum (zoo) within the park. Visitor details still require official-source review.

details.imageAlt: Designed by the storied local firm of Esenwein & Johnson is the Buffalo Zoo's Elephant House. A Colonial Revival-style structure of Roman brick with Indiana limestone trim, the building is topped by an unusual but charming octagonal cupola decorated with latticed windows, features a proud bust of an elephant head sculpted by Ira Lake, and betrays an Arts & Crafts influence with the widely overhanging, bracket-supported eaves of its side-gabled roof. A state-of-the-art facility at the time of its construction in 1912, it was considered outdated (and was a flashpoint of criticism by animal rights advocates, who claimed that housing elephants in such a cramped space was cruel) by the time the Zoo relocated its two remaining elephants in 2018.

details.imageAlt: A panoramic view from the overlook of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial at Highland Park in Rochester, New York, as seen on a May 2022 afternoon. Dedicated in 1996, the memorial is comprised principally of a concrete plaza where seven flagpoles - the American flag, those of the five branches of the U.S. armed forces, and the official POW/MIA flag - cluster around a sculpture of the globe carved in relief into the ground, highlighting the physical distance and lack of obvious connection between the U.S. and Vietnam, from which leads a "Walk of Honor" where 280 bollards bear the names, military insignia, and dates of birth and death of local Vietnam War casualties. Peppered around the sprawling grounds of the memorial are a number of other sculptures and gardens each paying respect to a different aspect of the phenomenon of military service and death in war.

features.name: King Memorial Fountain
features.description: King Memorial Fountain is a mapped landmark (memorial) within the park. Visitor details still require official-source review.

details.imageAlt: Visitors to Washington Park in Albany, New York on a May 2022 afternoon mill around the 1893 statue Moses Smiting the Rock while awaiting the beginning of the 5:30 PM Tulip Tour, the last one of the season before the official start of the 2022 Tulip Festival. A work of New York sculptor John Massey Rhind, the statue is a commission of J. Howard King who bequeathed $20,000 for its construction as a memorial to his father, banking magnate Rufus Howard King (1794-1967; not to be confused with the similarly named former U.S. Vice-President), hence its alternate name, the King Memorial Fountain. Atop a boulder taken from Storm King Mountain on the Hudson River is placed a 3,800-pound, larger-than-life bronze likeness of Moses with staff held triumphantly aloft, having smitten the Rock of Horeb to provide drinking water for the Israelites as told in Exodus 17:6. Surrounding Moses as the base of the rock are a quartet of smaller figures, including a maiden with water jug in hand (left) and a thin beaded man with arms outstretched (right) , representative of youth and old age respectively. As seen on a May 2022 evening.

features.description: Neill Log House is a mapped landmark (building) within the park. Visitor details still require official-source review.

details.imageAlt: Neill Log House located at East Circuit Road near Serpentine Drive in Schenley Park in the Squirrel Hill South neighborhood of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania , on April 10, 2010. The log house was built circa 1787 (or before) and once belonged to the family of Robert Neill, and later to Col. James O'Hara and his granddaughter Mary Schenley (for whom the park is named). The house was in use during a time when Indian raids in the area occasionally occurred. These days it sits preserved in Schenley Park with a fence around it (though it is open to the public periodically), and it is on the List of City of Pittsburgh historic designations as well as the List of Pittsburgh History and Landmarks Foundation Historic Landmarks . The log house is also featured on the cover of A Guidebook To Historic Western Pennsylvania by Helene Smith and George Swetnam (the original 1976 version and the Revised 1991 version).
